title: Fathers and Daughters 2: How Fathers Can Show Up for Their Daughters
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: This is the second entry in Anthony Bradley's serialized commentary on fatherhood, working through chapter two of Susan Swartz's The Absent Father Effects on Daughters. Bradley's framing device is that the chapter, ostensibly about absent fathers, functions in reverse as a practical guide to being present: every failure Swartz documents is the mirror image of something a father could actively choose to do instead. The piece opens with Swartz's claim that father-daughter estrangement is often generational, since fathers who struggle to connect with their own daughters frequently never had an affectionate relationship with their own fathers. Working through several of Swartz's clinical vignettes, Bradley draws out specific, actionable principles: give understanding without demanding she prove her case first, don't create distance and then act surprised she noticed it, give attention that isn't conditional on her achievements, and stay present through every developmental phase rather than connecting early and withdrawing at adolescence. The full piece continues as a list of sixteen father-daughter principles; this excerpt covers the framing and the first four.
points: Drawing on Susan Swartz's The Absent Father Effects on Daughters, the piece frames fatherlessness as often generational: fathers who struggle to connect with daughters frequently had no affectionate relationship with their own fathers.
Daughters internalize a father's emotional distance as something wrong with themselves rather than a failure on the father's part, which is why unexplained withdrawal does lasting relational damage.

Attention that has to be earned through achievement teaches daughters to associate their father's warmth with performance and its withdrawal with failure, rather than experiencing unconditional presence.
Fathers who connect early but withdraw during adolescence repeat the same core wound at a new developmental stage, since daughters need consistent presence through every phase.
quotes: Generations of fathers who had trouble developing and maintaining loving relationships with their daughters also never had affectionate relationships with their own fathers.

Susan Schwartz's chapter "Loss and Longing" could almost be titled "What Father's Should Not Do." It's constructed almost entirely around fathers who are absent emotionally, physically or both. Read backwards, it's a subtle how-to on being present.

When Hailey came to therapy, she had been avoiding her father for years without recognizing that absence was what she was avoiding. Daughters internalize distance from their fathers as something wrong with them, rather than him.
Loss and Longing makes clear that daughters who have to "earn" their fathers attention come to equate such attention with failure. "The good feeling does not last, and any good is followed by bad.

Mother-daughter relationships get a lot of press, but fathers are critical at every stage. Schwartz gives examples of dads who connect with daughters early only to withdraw during teenage years, and vice-versa.
Ask her about her day. Listen long enough that she doesn't have to repeat herself. Don't ask her to have all the answers before she approaches you with a question.
